column2: From Abū Masʿūd al-Badrī (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Among the words of the earliest prophecy that people have received is: If you feel no shame, then do as you wish.” Al-Bukhārī reported it.
Al-Bukhārī recorded this hadith through the narration of Manṣūr ibn al-Muʿtamir, from Ribʿī ibn Ḥirāsh, from Abū Masʿūd, from the Prophet ﷺ. I think Muslim did not record it

because some narrators reported it saying, “from Ribʿī, from Ḥudhayfah, from the Prophet ﷺ,” so there is disagreement over its chain. Most of the ḥāfiẓ scholars, however, judged the correct version to be that of those who said

“from Abū Masʿūd” — among them al-Bukhārī, Abū Zurʿah al-Rāzī, al-Dāraquṭnī and others. What shows this to be correct is that it has been narrated by another route from Abū Masʿūd, through Masrūq's narration from him.
Al-Ṭabarānī also recorded it from the hadith of Abū al-Ṭufayl, from the Prophet ﷺ.

His words ﷺ, “Among the words of the earliest prophecy that people have received,” indicate that this saying has been handed down from the earlier prophets, and that people passed it around among themselves

and inherited it from them generation after generation. This shows that the earlier prophecies brought this saying, and that it became so widely known among people that it reached the first generation of this nation.
In some narrations he said: “People have received nothing of the words of the earliest prophecy except this.”
Ḥumayd ibn Zanjawayh and others recorded it.
As for his words, “If you feel no shame, then do as you wish,” there are two views on their meaning.
The first is that it is not a command in the sense that one should do whatever one wishes; rather, it is meant as censure and prohibition. Those who hold this view take one of two approaches.

The first is that it is a command meant as a threat and a warning, the sense being: If you have no shame, do whatever you wish, for Allah will requite you for it. It is like His words, “Do whatever you wish; indeed, He sees what you do” [Fuṣṣilat 41:40], and His words,

“So worship whatever you wish besides Him” [al-Zumar 39:15], and the words of the Prophet ﷺ, “Whoever sells wine, let him butcher pigs” — that is, let him cut them up, either to sell them or to eat them. There are many examples of this. It is the view chosen by a group, among them Abū al-ʿAbbās Thaʿlab.

The second approach is that it is a command in form but a statement in meaning; the sense is that whoever has no shame will do whatever he wishes. For what restrains a person from shameful deeds is modesty (ḥayāʾ), so whoever has no modesty
plunges into every indecency and evil, and into the like of what a person with modesty refrains from. It is along the lines of his words ﷺ, “Whoever lies about me deliberately,

let him take his seat in the Fire”: the wording is that of a command, but the meaning is a statement — that whoever lies about him will take his seat in the Fire. This is the view chosen by Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām (may Allah have mercy on him),
Ibn Qutaybah, Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī and others, and Abū Dāwūd narrated from Imam Aḥmad what points to a view like this.

Ibn Lahīʿah narrated, from Abū Qabīl, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “When Allah hates a servant, He strips him of modesty. When He has stripped him of modesty, you will find him only hating and hated.

And He strips him of trustworthiness; when He has stripped him of trustworthiness, He strips him of mercy; when He has stripped him of mercy, He strips him of the tether of Islam; and when He has stripped him of the tether of Islam, you will find him only a rebellious devil.”
Ḥumayd ibn Zanjawayh recorded it. Ibn Mājah also recorded it in meaning, with a weak chain, from Ibn ʿUmar, likewise as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ).

Salmān al-Fārisī said: When Allah wills the destruction of a servant, He strips him of modesty. When He has stripped him of modesty, you will find him only detestable and detested. When he is detestable and detested, He strips him of trustworthiness, and you will find him only treacherous and distrusted.

When he is treacherous and distrusted, He strips him of mercy, and you will find him only harsh and hard-hearted. When he is harsh and hard-hearted, He removes the tether of faith from his neck; and when He has removed the tether of faith from his neck, you will find him only a devil, accursed and execrated.
Ibn ʿAbbās said: Modesty and faith are tied together on one rope; when modesty is removed, the other follows it.
Ḥumayd ibn Zanjawayh recorded all of this in Kitāb al-Adab.
The Prophet ﷺ made modesty part of faith, as in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from Ibn ʿUmar: the Prophet ﷺ passed by a man who was reproaching his brother about his modesty, saying:
You are so shy — as if to say: it has done you harm. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Leave him, for modesty is part of faith.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, he said: “Modesty is a branch of faith.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Modesty brings nothing but good.” In a narration of Muslim's he said: “Modesty is good, all of it,” or he said: “Modesty, all of it, is good.”
Imam Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of al-Ashajj al-ʿAṣarī, that he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: “You have two traits that Allah loves.” I said: What are they?
He said: “Forbearance and modesty.” I said: Have I had them from long ago, or are they new?
He said: “From long ago.” I said: Praise be to Allah, who has formed me with two traits that Allah loves.

Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid said: ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn came in to the Prophet ﷺ while a man was with him. The man asked for a drink; water was brought and he drank, and the Prophet ﷺ screened him. ʿUyaynah said: What is this?
He said: “Modesty — a trait they have been given and you have been denied.”
Know that modesty is of two kinds.

The first is part of one's created nature and disposition, not acquired. It is one of the noblest traits of character that Allah grants a servant and forms him upon. That is why he ﷺ said, “Modesty brings nothing but good,” for it holds one back from shameful deeds and base character,

and urges one to practise noble and lofty traits of character; in this respect it is one of the qualities of faith. It has been narrated that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Whoever feels shame keeps himself hidden; whoever keeps himself hidden is wary; and whoever is wary is protected.
Al-Jarrāḥ ibn ʿAbdillāh al-Ḥakamī, the foremost horseman of the people of al-Shām, said: I left sins out of shame for forty years, and then scrupulousness (waraʿ) came to me.
Someone said: I saw sins as base, so I left them out of self-respect (murūʾah), and that turned into religion.
The second is acquired from knowing Allah: knowing His greatness, His nearness to His servants, His awareness of them, and His knowledge of the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal.
This is among the highest qualities of faith; indeed, it is among the highest degrees of excellence (iḥsān). It has been mentioned earlier that the Prophet ﷺ said to a man:
“Be shy of Allah as you would be shy of a righteous man of your own clan.”

In the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd: “Being shy of Allah is to guard the head and what it holds, and the belly and what it contains, and to remember death and decay. Whoever wants the Hereafter leaves the adornment of this world. Whoever does that has been shy of Allah.” Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded it as marfūʿ.

Modesty before Allah may also be born of contemplating His blessings and seeing one's shortcomings in thanking Him for them. When a servant is stripped of both acquired and innate modesty, nothing remains to restrain him from shameful deeds and base character, and he becomes as though he had no faith.

It has been narrated among the mursal reports of al-Ḥasan that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Modesty is of two kinds: one is a part of faith, and the other is incapacity” — though perhaps these are al-Ḥasan's own words. Similarly, Bushayr ibn Kaʿb al-ʿAdawī said to ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn:

We find in some books that part of it is tranquillity and gravity for Allah's sake, and part of it is weakness. ʿImrān grew angry and said: I tell you something from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and you set something against it?
The matter is as ʿImrān (may Allah be pleased with him) said, for the modesty praised in the words of the Prophet ﷺ means only the trait of character that urges one to do what is fine

and leave what is shameful. As for the weakness and incapacity that make one fall short in any of the rights of Allah or the rights of His servants, that is not modesty at all; it is only weakness and feebleness, incapacity and abjectness. And Allah knows best.

The second view on the meaning of his words, “If you feel no shame, then do as you wish,” is that it is a command to do whatever one wishes, according to the outward sense of the words, and that the meaning is:
If what you want to do is something one need not be ashamed of doing, neither before Allah nor before people, because it is an act of obedience

or a matter of fine character and approved manners, then do of it whatever you wish. This is the view of a group of imams, among them Abū Isḥāq al-Marwazī the Shāfiʿī. Something similar is related from Imam Aḥmad, and it appears so in some copies of the abridgement of the Masāʾil that Abū Dāwūd related from him;

but what is in the reliable, complete copies is as we related from him earlier, and that is how al-Khallāl narrated it from him in Kitāb al-Adab. Of this kind is the saying of one of the Salaf, when asked about self-respect (murūʾah):

That you do nothing in private that you would be ashamed of in public. The Prophet's words ﷺ, “Sin is what wavers in your breast and you dislike people to see,” will come in their proper place in this book, if Allah the Exalted wills.
ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated in his book, from Maʿmar, from Abū Isḥāq, from a man of Muzaynah, who said: It was said: Messenger of Allah, what is the best thing a Muslim man has been given?
He said: “Good character.” The man said: Then what is the worst thing a Muslim has been given?
He said: “If you would dislike something to be seen on you in people's gathering, do not do it when you are alone.”
In the Ṣaḥīḥ of Ibn Ḥibbān, from Usāmah ibn Sharīk, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“Whatever Allah dislikes from you, do not do it when you are alone.”
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī, that he said: I said: Messenger of Allah, what is the completion of righteousness?
He said: “That you do in private what you do in public.”
He also recorded it from the hadith of Abū ʿĀmir al-Sakūnī, who said: I said: Messenger of Allah — and he mentioned it.
The ḥāfiẓ ʿAbd al-Ghanī ibn Saʿīd narrated in his book Adab al-Muḥaddith, with his chain, from Ḥarmalah ibn ʿAbdillāh, who said:
I came to the Prophet ﷺ to increase in knowledge. I stood before him and said: Messenger of Allah, what do you command me to act upon?
He said: “Do what is right and avoid what is wrong. Look at whatever good you hear people say of you when you have got up to leave them, and do it;

and look at what you would dislike people to say of you when you have got up to leave them, and avoid it.” He said: I looked, and found that they were two things that left nothing out: doing what is right and avoiding what is wrong.
Ibn Saʿd recorded it in meaning in his Ṭabaqāt.

Abū ʿUbayd related another view on the meaning of the hadith, which he related from Jarīr: Its meaning is that a man wants to do some good and leaves it out of shame before people, as though he fears showing off. He is saying: do not let shame stop you from going ahead with what you intended,

as in the hadith: “If Satan comes to you while you are praying and says, ‘You are showing off,’ then make it longer.” Then Abū ʿUbayd said: Neither the context nor the wording of this hadith fits this interpretation, nor do people understand it so.

I say: Had it been as Jarīr said, the wording of the hadith would have been: “If you feel shame at what one need not be ashamed of, then do as you wish.” How far this is from the wording and meaning of the hadith is plain. And Allah knows best.
